questions.prompt: A process is in the ready queue when a higher-priority process arrives. Which transition occurs immediately under a preemptive scheduler?
answer: running to ready
questions.explanation: The arrival can cause the current process to lose the CPU, but it remains eligible to run. It is preempted into ready; it has not requested I/O.

questions.prompt: A process blocks on disk I/O. When the I/O completes, what is its state before it next receives CPU time?
answer: ready
questions.explanation: Completion makes the process eligible to compete for the CPU. It cannot become running directly unless dispatch also occurs.

questions.prompt: A process is waiting for a child, but the child has not exited. Which state best describes the parent?
answer: blocked
questions.explanation: The parent cannot make progress until the wait condition is satisfied, so it is blocked. It is not merely ready because an event is required.

questions.prompt: A process has finished execution, but its parent has not collected its exit status. Which description applies in Unix-like systems?
answer: zombie
questions.explanation: The terminated process retains a small kernel record containing its PID and status until reaped. Its address space and execution are gone.

questions.prompt: A parent terminates while its child continues running. The child is commonly called a(n):
answer: orphan
questions.explanation: An orphan is a living child whose parent has exited. A zombie has already terminated and awaits status collection.

questions.prompt: Which item is normally saved in a process context switch?
answer: program counter and general registers
questions.explanation: The CPU register state, including the program counter and stack pointer, must be preserved to resume execution. Memory need not be copied on every switch.

questions.prompt: Two processes share the same code pages but have separate writable data. Which mechanism can provide this after fork efficiently?
answer: copy-on-write
questions.explanation: Copy-on-write initially maps pages read-only and duplicates a page only when a writer attempts modification. This avoids copying untouched data.

questions.prompt: After a successful fork, which statement about the return value is correct?
options: It is zero in the child and the child PID in the parent
It is the parent PID in both processes
It is zero in both processes
It is the child PID in the child and zero in the parent
answer: It is zero in the child and the child PID in the parent
questions.explanation: The return value distinguishes the two execution paths: zero identifies the child, while the parent receives the new child PID.

questions.prompt: A process calls exec successfully. What happens to its process identity?
options: PID stays the same while the program image is replaced
A new PID is always allocated
answer: PID stays the same while the program image is replaced
questions.explanation: Exec overlays the calling process image with a new program. It does not itself create a process, so the PID remains unchanged.

questions.prompt: A child exits, and the parent calls wait. Which result is guaranteed if wait succeeds?
options: The child is reaped and its exit status can be collected
answer: The child is reaped and its exit status can be collected
questions.explanation: Wait collects termination status for one child and releases its zombie record. It does not restart the child or reap arbitrary descendants.

questions.prompt: A process executes fork once, and both parent and child then execute a second unconditional fork. Assuming all calls succeed, how many processes exist at the end?
questions.explanation: Each of the two existing processes creates one child in the second fork. The population doubles from two to four.

questions.prompt: Three successive unconditional fork calls are executed by every process created so far. How many total processes result, including the original?
questions.explanation: Each fork doubles the population: 1 ? 2 ? 4 ? 8. This count includes the original process.

questions.prompt: A program forks once inside an if condition that is true only in the parent (the child branch skips the condition body). How many processes exist afterward?
questions.explanation: Only the original process reaches the fork, so one child is created. The child?s later control flow does not re-enter the already tested condition.

questions.prompt: A parent has two children. One exits; the other is still running. A wait call returns successfully. What can be concluded?
options: At least one terminated child was collected
The parent has no children now
answer: At least one terminated child was collected
questions.explanation: A successful wait can return for an already terminated child while another child continues. The second child remains the parent?s child.

questions.prompt: A child invokes _exit(7). What is the value typically made available to its parent through wait status decoding?
questions.explanation: The low-order exit status supplied to _exit is reported to the parent (subject to the platform?s status encoding and extraction macros).

questions.prompt: A process is preempted by a timer interrupt. Which state transition is most appropriate if it remains runnable?
answer: running to ready
questions.explanation: A timer interrupt ends the process?s current CPU turn without making it wait for an event. The scheduler places it back in the ready state.

questions.prompt: Which pair of resources is typically per-process rather than shared among all processes?
options: virtual address space and register context
answer: virtual address space and register context
questions.explanation: A process has its own virtual address space and saved CPU context. Physical hardware and kernel code are system-wide resources.

questions.prompt: A process is waiting for a page fault to be serviced from disk. Which state is most suitable?
answer: blocked
questions.explanation: The process cannot continue until the faulting page arrives, so it waits on an I/O-related event. After completion it returns to ready.

questions.prompt: A process is admitted to memory and is eligible to run but has never received the CPU. Its state is:
answer: ready
questions.explanation: The ready state means the process can execute as soon as selected. Running specifically means it currently owns a CPU.

questions.prompt: A process terminates while holding a user-space mutex. What does process termination by itself guarantee about that mutex?
options: Nothing about a shared mutex?s consistency is guaranteed
The OS always unlocks it safely for all processes
The mutex is converted to a semaphore
answer: Nothing about a shared mutex?s consistency is guaranteed
questions.explanation: A process dying while holding a process-shared lock can leave application state inconsistent. Kernel cleanup of resources does not automatically repair arbitrary user-level synchronization.

questions.prompt: A fork occurs while a thread library process has several threads. In POSIX-style semantics, which is the usual result in the child?
options: Only the calling thread exists in the child
All threads are copied and run independently
answer: Only the calling thread exists in the child
questions.explanation: After fork in a multithreaded process, the child contains only the thread that called fork. This is why the child typically calls exec promptly.

questions.prompt: A process calls fork, then the child calls exec. Which memory behavior best describes the child?
options: Its old address-space image is replaced by the new program image
It keeps all old mappings and appends a new stack
It becomes a thread of the parent
answer: Its old address-space image is replaced by the new program image
questions.explanation: Exec replaces code, data, heap, and stack mappings with those for the new program while preserving process identity.

questions.prompt: Which operation creates a new process in the classic Unix process model?
answer: fork
questions.explanation: Fork creates a child process. Exec changes the executing program, wait synchronizes with a child, and exit terminates the caller.

questions.prompt: A parent calls waitpid for a specific child that is still running, without a nonblocking option. What does the parent do?
options: Blocks until that child changes state in a waitable way
Returns immediately with the child?s future PID
answer: Blocks until that child changes state in a waitable way
questions.explanation: A blocking waitpid waits for the specified child?s relevant state change, usually termination. It does not execute the child or terminate it.

questions.prompt: A process table entry is needed after a process exits mainly to preserve:
options: the PID and termination status for the parent
all its open file data copied into RAM
answer: the PID and termination status for the parent
questions.explanation: The zombie record holds minimal bookkeeping so the parent can obtain the exit status and the PID can be managed correctly. The process cannot resume.

questions.prompt: A process performs a blocking read from an empty pipe. What transition normally occurs?
options: blocked to running without an event
answer: running to blocked
questions.explanation: A blocking read waits for data, yielding the CPU while the process is blocked. Data arrival makes it ready; dispatch later makes it running.

questions.prompt: A context switch from P to Q occurs. Which statement is correct?
options: The kernel saves P?s CPU state and restores Q?s saved state
P?s entire memory is copied into Q
The switch necessarily requires disk I/O
answer: The kernel saves P?s CPU state and restores Q?s saved state
questions.explanation: A context switch changes the executing context by saving and restoring registers and related scheduling state. It need not copy memory or access disk.

questions.prompt: A process has two children, both terminated and unreaped. How many zombie processes may exist?
questions.explanation: Each terminated child can retain a separate zombie record until its exit status is collected. Thus both can be zombies simultaneously.

questions.prompt: A child exits before its parent calls wait. What happens to the child in the interval?
options: It remains a zombie until reaped
It continues executing as an orphan
It is converted to a ready process
answer: It remains a zombie until reaped
questions.explanation: The child has terminated and cannot execute, but its minimal exit record is retained until the parent collects it. That state is zombie.

questions.prompt: A process forks and both branches increment a private integer initialized to 5. After each branch increments once, what value does each process observe?
answer: 6 in each process
questions.explanation: Fork gives the child a logically separate address space. Each branch changes its own copy, so both observe 6 rather than sharing a single increment.

questions.prompt: A process has one child that is a zombie and another child that is still blocked on I/O. A successful wait can reap:
answer: the zombie child only
questions.explanation: A normal wait reports a child that has terminated. The blocked child is still alive, so it cannot be reaped.

questions.prompt: After fork, parent and child share a file descriptor referring to the same open file description. Which state is commonly shared?
answer: the open-file offset
questions.explanation: Duplicated descriptors can refer to the same open-file description, so file offset and status flags may be shared. The processes still have distinct PIDs and memory contexts.

questions.prompt: A child closes a descriptor after fork. What is generally true of the parent?s descriptor?
options: It remains open in the parent
The child?s entire descriptor table is destroyed in the parent
answer: It remains open in the parent
questions.explanation: Each process has its own descriptor table after fork; closing one descriptor entry does not close the other process?s entry, though the underlying open-file reference count changes.

questions.prompt: Which event normally moves a process from blocked to ready?
options: completion of the event it was waiting for
answer: completion of the event it was waiting for
questions.explanation: An awaited event such as I/O completion makes the process eligible to run. The scheduler may dispatch it later, but dispatch is a separate ready-to-running transition.

questions.prompt: A process issues a nonblocking read when no data is available. Relative to a blocking read, the process typically:
options: remains runnable and receives an immediate no-data result
answer: remains runnable and receives an immediate no-data result
questions.explanation: A nonblocking operation returns promptly when it cannot proceed. The process can continue executing rather than sleeping for data.

questions.prompt: A process is ready, and the CPU is idle. What action changes its state to running?
answer: dispatch
questions.explanation: The dispatcher selects a ready process for a CPU. Admission moves a new process into the system; I/O completion usually moves blocked to ready.

questions.prompt: A process is swapped out while waiting for an event. In a suspended-state model, its state is best represented as:
answer: blocked-suspended
questions.explanation: It is both waiting for an event and not resident in main memory, hence blocked-suspended. When the event occurs it can become ready-suspended.

questions.prompt: A process is swapped out but is otherwise eligible to execute. Its state is:
answer: ready-suspended
questions.explanation: It is ready to run but not currently resident, so ready-suspended captures both facts. It cannot actually execute until brought back into memory.

questions.prompt: Which action is usually performed by the short-term scheduler?
options: selecting a ready process for the CPU
admitting jobs from the job pool
answer: selecting a ready process for the CPU
questions.explanation: The short-term scheduler chooses among ready processes for immediate CPU execution. Long-term admission and memory replacement are separate functions.

questions.prompt: A process control block typically stores which scheduling information?
answer: process state and priority
questions.explanation: The PCB stores state needed to manage and resume the process, including scheduling parameters such as priority and queue links. Program text is represented by address-space mappings.

questions.prompt: At fork, the child receives a distinct PID. Which identifier is normally inherited from the parent?
options: current instruction pointer value as a permanently shared register
answer: current working directory
questions.explanation: The child inherits environment and process attributes such as current working directory, subject to platform semantics. It gets its own PID, and its parent PID identifies the original process.

questions.prompt: A child exits with status 256 on a system that exposes only the low 8 bits of the exit code. What status value is available?
questions.explanation: Only the low eight bits are retained in this conventional interface. Since 256 is 0 modulo 256, the reported exit code is zero.

questions.prompt: A parent uses waitpid(child, ..., WNOHANG) while the child is still running. What is the usual result?
options: It returns immediately indicating no child state is ready
It blocks until the child exits
It returns the child?s final status
answer: It returns immediately indicating no child state is ready
questions.explanation: WNOHANG requests a nonblocking check. If the child has no reportable state change, waitpid returns immediately with an indication that nothing is ready.

questions.prompt: Which pair of operations is commonly combined to launch a different program as a child?
answer: fork followed by exec
questions.explanation: Fork creates the child; exec then replaces its program image. This separation allows the parent to retain its own image and optionally wait.

questions.prompt: A process creates a child and then exits without waiting. What is the child?s status immediately after the parent exits?
options: It is still a live process and becomes an orphan
It must be terminated with the parent
answer: It is still a live process and becomes an orphan
questions.explanation: The child?s execution is independent after creation. When its parent exits, it is an orphan and is typically adopted by a system reaper.

questions.prompt: A process invokes exit while another thread in the same process is running. Under ordinary process-wide exit semantics, what happens?
options: The process terminates, including its other threads
Only the calling thread terminates and the process continues
The caller becomes a zombie thread while the process runs
The kernel forks a replacement process
answer: The process terminates, including its other threads
questions.explanation: Process termination ends the process as a whole, so its threads cease as well. A thread-only exit primitive has different semantics.

questions.prompt: A context switch takes 4 microseconds. A CPU-bound process is switched out and later back in once per quantum. Ignoring other overheads, what context-switch time is charged per quantum cycle?
answer: 8 microseconds
questions.explanation: One switch saves the process and dispatches another; a later switch restores it. The two transitions cost 2 ? 4 = 8 microseconds.

questions.prompt: The same process is preempted 25 times, and each switch costs 3 microseconds. Total time spent in these switch operations is:
answer: 75 microseconds
questions.explanation: Each preemption corresponds to one context-switch operation under the stated accounting. Thus 25 ? 3 = 75 microseconds.

questions.prompt: A parent remains alive, creates four children, and does not call wait. All four children exit. How many child zombie records can be pending for this parent?
questions.explanation: Each of the four terminated children may retain a separate status record because the parent has not reaped them. The living parent is not itself a zombie.

questions.prompt: A process in ready state is not executing because:
options: it is waiting for CPU allocation
it is waiting for I/O completion
answer: it is waiting for CPU allocation
questions.explanation: Ready means runnable but not currently assigned a CPU. Waiting for I/O is blocked; termination ends execution.

questions.prompt: A process calls fork and checks for a negative return value. If fork fails, which execution fact is correct?
options: No child was created by that call
A child exists but has PID zero
The parent has already been replaced
Both processes continue after the call
answer: No child was created by that call
questions.explanation: A failed fork reports an error to the caller and does not create a child. Code must handle failure before assuming two execution paths exist.

questions.prompt: A process group receives a termination signal. Which statement about process identity is correct?
options: A process group is a collection of processes with distinct PIDs
All group members become one process
The group ID replaces every member PID
Only parent and child can belong to a group
answer: A process group is a collection of processes with distinct PIDs
questions.explanation: A process group supports signal and job-control operations over a set of processes; each member remains an individual process with its own PID.

questions.prompt: A child process calls getppid after its parent has exited and it has been adopted. What does getppid report?
options: The PID of the adopting parent
The PID of the original parent forever
answer: The PID of the adopting parent
questions.explanation: After adoption, the kernel updates the child?s parent relationship. getppid reports the current parent, not necessarily the process that originally forked it.

questions.prompt: A process is in the new state. Which event most directly moves it to ready?
options: Admission into the set of executable processes
answer: Admission into the set of executable processes
questions.explanation: Admission makes a newly created process eligible for scheduling. I/O completion is for blocked processes; time-slice expiration affects a running process.

questions.prompt: A process has been selected for execution but has not yet run because the CPU is finishing a mode transition. Conceptually, after dispatch it is:
answer: running
questions.explanation: Dispatch is the transition from ready to running. The actual first instruction may occur after a small implementation delay.

questions.prompt: Which description best captures a process image?
options: The executable code, data, stack, heap, and related execution context
Only the source file on disk
Every page in physical memory, including other processes
answer: The executable code, data, stack, heap, and related execution context
questions.explanation: The process image refers to the program?s execution representation, including its address-space regions and execution context. A PCB is management metadata rather than the whole image.

questions.prompt: A process changes its priority while waiting in the ready queue. What remains true?
options: It is still ready until dispatched or blocked by another event
It becomes blocked because its priority changed
answer: It is still ready until dispatched or blocked by another event
questions.explanation: Priority affects scheduling choice but does not by itself change the process?s readiness. A dispatcher must still assign a CPU.

questions.prompt: The kernel performs a system call for a process and returns to the same process without scheduling another one. Is this necessarily a process context switch?
options: No; a privilege-mode switch can occur without changing processes
Yes; every system call switches processes
Yes; entering the kernel creates a child
No; system calls execute only in user mode
answer: No; a privilege-mode switch can occur without changing processes
questions.explanation: A system call crosses from user to kernel mode, but the same process may resume afterward. A process context switch occurs only if execution changes to another process.

questions.prompt: A process is interrupted, and the kernel resumes the same process after handling the interrupt. Which claim is correct?
options: An interrupt does not necessarily cause a process context switch
Every interrupt creates a new process
answer: An interrupt does not necessarily cause a process context switch
questions.explanation: Interrupt handling may return to the interrupted process. Whether a context switch happens depends on scheduling decisions and events, not merely on the interrupt.

questions.prompt: A child calls exec but the executable cannot be loaded. What normally happens to the calling process?
options: Exec returns an error and the old image remains active
The PID changes and a blank image runs
The process becomes a zombie immediately
answer: Exec returns an error and the old image remains active
questions.explanation: A failed exec does not complete the image replacement, so it returns an error to the caller, which can continue in its old program image.

questions.prompt: A parent performs wait and two children have already exited. How many can one ordinary wait reap?
answer: One
questions.explanation: A single wait call reports one terminated child. The parent must call wait again to collect another child?s status.

questions.prompt: A process calls wait when it has no unwaited-for children. What is the usual behavior?
options: It returns the PID of its parent
answer: It returns an error
questions.explanation: Waiting is meaningful only for a child relationship. If there is no eligible child, wait reports an error rather than blocking forever.

questions.prompt: A program forks in a loop that runs exactly k times in each process created by prior iterations. How many processes exist after k iterations?
questions.explanation: Every existing process forks once per iteration, so the count doubles each time. After k doublings, the total including the original is 2^k.

questions.prompt: In a loop, each process forks once, but only the child exits immediately and the parent continues to the next iteration. Starting with one process, after 4 iterations how many live loop participants remain?
questions.explanation: At each iteration the existing parent creates one child that immediately exits, while the original parent alone continues. Thus one process reaches each next iteration.

questions.prompt: A parent forks twice sequentially and neither child forks. How many children does it have at the end?
questions.explanation: Each fork is executed only by the original parent because no child forks. Therefore it creates two children, for three total processes.

questions.prompt: A process forks, and both branches fork again, but only the original parent performs a third fork. How many total processes result?
questions.explanation: First fork yields two processes, second executed by both yields four, and the final fork by only the original adds one. Total: 4 + 1 + 2 existing descendants created earlier = 7.

questions.prompt: A process forks once. The parent waits before printing, while the child prints and exits. What ordering is guaranteed?
options: The child?s print occurs before the parent?s post-wait print
The two prints must occur simultaneously
The child cannot print until the parent exits
answer: The child?s print occurs before the parent?s post-wait print
questions.explanation: The parent is blocked in wait until the child exits, so the child?s print and termination precede the parent continuing after wait.

questions.prompt: Two sibling processes both write to the same pipe, and the parent waits for one child. What does wait guarantee about output ordering between siblings?
options: No total ordering between sibling output is guaranteed
The child created first always writes first
The parent serializes sibling writes automatically
The second child is blocked until the first exits
answer: No total ordering between sibling output is guaranteed
questions.explanation: Waiting for one child constrains the parent, not the relative schedule of siblings. Their writes can interleave or arrive in either order, subject to write atomicity rules.

questions.prompt: A process is marked stopped after receiving a job-control stop signal. Which statement is most accurate?
options: It is not eligible to run until continued
It is terminated and can never resume
It is blocked only on disk I/O
answer: It is not eligible to run until continued
questions.explanation: A stopped process is suspended from execution but retains its state and can resume after a continue event. This differs from termination and zombie status.

questions.prompt: A process receives a signal whose default action is termination. Before the parent reaps it, the process is:
options: terminated, possibly represented as a zombie
answer: terminated, possibly represented as a zombie
questions.explanation: With the default terminating action, execution ceases. Until status is collected, the kernel may retain a zombie record for the parent.

questions.prompt: A single process executes 5 unconditional fork calls in sequence; every process created continues to execute the remaining calls. How many processes exist at the end?
questions.explanation: Each of five calls doubles the population, so the final count is 2^5 = 32, including the original process.

questions.prompt: A process forks once. Only the parent executes one additional fork afterward; each child exits before that second call. How many total processes were created, counting the original?
questions.explanation: The first fork creates one child. The parent alone executes the second fork and creates another child, giving three distinct processes in total.

questions.prompt: A parent has 3 children that all terminate without being waited for. How many child exit records can be waiting for collection?
questions.explanation: Each exited child can leave one unreaped status record. Since all three children have terminated and the parent has not waited, three records may be pending.

questions.prompt: A process executes fork in a loop for 4 iterations, with every process continuing the loop. How many fork calls in total are executed?
questions.explanation: The number of calls per iteration is 1, 2, 4, and 8. Their sum is 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15.

questions.prompt: A parent creates 6 children sequentially. Each child exits immediately, and the parent reaps each child before creating the next. What is the maximum number of simultaneously existing processes including the parent?
questions.explanation: At each point the parent and at most one newly created child coexist. The child is reaped before the next is created, so the maximum is two.

questions.prompt: A process forks 3 times in an if branch that only the original parent can reach. How many children does it create?
questions.explanation: Only the original parent executes each of the three fork calls. Each successful call creates one child, for three children.

questions.prompt: A running process is preempted 12 times. Each context-switch operation costs 5 microseconds. What is the total cost of those 12 operations in microseconds?
questions.explanation: The stated count is 12 switch operations, each costing 5 microseconds. Total overhead is 12 ? 5 = 60 microseconds.

questions.prompt: A process performs 4 fork calls in sequence, but after every call only the child continues and the parent exits. How many live processes remain after the fourth call?
questions.explanation: Each fork produces two branches, but the parent branch exits at every step. Exactly one child continues to the next iteration, leaving one live process at the end.

questions.prompt: A process creates 2 children. Each child creates 2 children of its own; the original parent creates no further children. How many processes are in the resulting tree, including the root?
questions.explanation: The tree has one root, two children, and four grandchildren. The total is 1 + 2 + 4 = 7.

questions.prompt: A parent waits for 4 children, all of which have exited. What is the minimum number of successful wait calls needed to collect all four exit statuses?
questions.explanation: One successful wait call collects one child?s status. Four terminated children therefore require four successful waits.

questions.prompt: Which properties are normally private to a process after a successful fork?
answer: its PID
its virtual address-space identity
its parent-child relationship
questions.explanation: Parent and child have distinct process identities and address spaces and distinct relationship metadata. They can run on the same CPU core over time, so the core is not a private process property.

questions.prompt: Which statements about exec are correct?
options: It replaces the caller?s program image on success
It normally preserves the process PID
It creates a child process by itself
It returns to the old image after successful replacement
answer: It replaces the caller?s program image on success
It normally preserves the process PID
questions.explanation: Exec overlays the current process image and retains its identity. It does not create a child, and a successful exec does not return to the old code path.

questions.prompt: Which events can move a process from running to ready?
options: blocking on an unavailable pipe read
answer: timer preemption
preemption by a higher-priority process
questions.explanation: Preemption leaves a process runnable, placing it in ready. An unavailable blocking read moves it to blocked, while exit terminates it.

questions.prompt: Which statements about a zombie are correct?
options: It may retain an exit status for its parent
A parent can remove its record by collecting its status
answer: It has terminated execution
It may retain an exit status for its parent
A parent can remove its record by collecting its status
questions.explanation: A zombie has no executing code and consumes no CPU. Its minimal status record remains until a parent or reaper collects it.

questions.prompt: Which resources are commonly inherited or duplicated across fork in Unix-like systems?
answer: environment variables
current working directory
open file descriptors
questions.explanation: The child inherits environment and working-directory state, and receives descriptor entries referring to open file descriptions. It receives a new PID.

questions.prompt: Which statements about process context switching are correct?
options: It saves enough CPU state to resume the outgoing process
It always copies the entire outgoing address space
It may occur after a timer interrupt
It is identical to every user-to-kernel mode transition
answer: It saves enough CPU state to resume the outgoing process
It may occur after a timer interrupt
questions.explanation: A context switch preserves CPU state and may be selected after a timer interrupt. It does not require copying the address space and is distinct from a mode switch.

questions.prompt: Which situations can leave a process blocked?
options: waiting in a blocking wait for a child
waiting for data on an empty blocking pipe
being eligible but not yet selected by the scheduler
answer: waiting for disk I/O completion
waiting in a blocking wait for a child
waiting for data on an empty blocking pipe
questions.explanation: The first three require an event before progress and are blocked conditions. A runnable process awaiting CPU time is ready, not blocked.

questions.prompt: Which statements about wait are correct?
options: A successful call can collect one terminated child
A blocking wait can suspend the caller while a child is still running
One call must collect all terminated children
A process with no eligible children can receive an error
answer: A successful call can collect one terminated child
A blocking wait can suspend the caller while a child is still running
A process with no eligible children can receive an error
questions.explanation: A wait operation reports one child?s status per successful call and can block until one is available. With no eligible child, it normally reports an error.

questions.prompt: Which outcomes are possible after a child exits before its parent?
options: The child is briefly a zombie
The child may be adopted if the parent exits
The child continues executing as an orphan
Its exit status can be collected by a wait operation
answer: The child is briefly a zombie
The child may be adopted if the parent exits
Its exit status can be collected by a wait operation
questions.explanation: An exited child can be a zombie and its parent can collect the status. If the parent also exits, an orphaned living child may be adopted; an exited child does not continue executing.

questions.prompt: Which statements about ready and blocked states are correct?
options: A ready process needs CPU allocation to run
A blocked process awaits an event
I/O completion commonly moves blocked to ready
A ready process is necessarily executing
answer: A ready process needs CPU allocation to run
A blocked process awaits an event
I/O completion commonly moves blocked to ready
questions.explanation: Ready means runnable but awaiting dispatch. Blocked means waiting for an event; its completion makes the process ready. Only running processes currently execute.

questions.prompt: A process creates two children. The parent waits for the first child specifically; that child exits, but the second remains blocked. Which statement is guaranteed?
options: The parent?s wait for the first child can return while the second remains alive
The parent must wait for both children before returning
The second child is automatically terminated
The first child becomes an orphan
answer: The parent?s wait for the first child can return while the second remains alive
questions.explanation: A wait targeting a particular child can complete when that child terminates. It imposes no requirement that a sibling also exit.

questions.prompt: A program has one process before entering a loop. Every iteration forks, but all children immediately exit and only the original parent continues. How does the number of loop iterations affect the final live-process count?
options: It increases by one per iteration
It is always the number of iterations
answer: It remains one
questions.explanation: Although a transient child is created each time, it exits before the next iteration. The original process is the sole continuing loop participant.

questions.prompt: A process has a pending child exit status. The parent calls wait and collects it. Which resource is released as a direct result?
options: The child?s executable file on disk
answer: The child?s retained termination record
questions.explanation: Reaping releases the kernel bookkeeping retained for the terminated child. It does not remove the parent?s memory or the executable file itself.

questions.prompt: A fork is followed by child code that changes a global variable. The parent reads its global afterward. What determines whether the parent sees the child?s change?
options: The child?s private address-space semantics prevent the write from changing the parent copy
The scheduler determines whether globals are shared
The parent sees it only if it waits
All globals are shared after fork
answer: The child?s private address-space semantics prevent the write from changing the parent copy
questions.explanation: The child and parent have separate logical address spaces after fork. A child?s ordinary write affects its own copy, regardless of scheduling or wait.

questions.prompt: A process is blocked for a child to exit. The child exits. What is the parent?s next scheduling state before it runs again?
answer: ready
questions.explanation: The event makes the parent eligible and moves it to ready. A later dispatch is required before it executes again.

questions.prompt: A process forks once and then both branches execute a print statement exactly once. How many prints occur?
questions.explanation: Both parent and child resume after the fork and each reaches the print once. Therefore there are two executions of the statement.

questions.prompt: A parent creates a child and then immediately calls exec itself. What happens to the already created child?
options: It remains a separate process; exec replaces only the parent image
The child is merged into the parent
The child is automatically reparented to itself
The child?s PID becomes the parent PID
answer: It remains a separate process; exec replaces only the parent image
questions.explanation: Exec changes the calling process?s image. It does not undo prior process creation or alter the independent child?s identity.

questions.prompt: A CPU-bound process is preempted at the end of its quantum and remains runnable. Which state transition occurs?
answer: running to ready
questions.explanation: Quantum expiration does not imply an event wait or termination. The process is placed back in the ready queue.

questions.prompt: A process makes a blocking system call for input. The device completes the request. Does the process execute immediately at completion?
options: No, it becomes ready and must be dispatched
Yes, completion directly gives it the CPU
answer: No, it becomes ready and must be dispatched
questions.explanation: I/O completion makes the process runnable, but CPU ownership is assigned separately by the scheduler. It enters ready before running.

questions.prompt: A child exits and is reaped. Can the parent later obtain that same child?s exit status with another wait?
options: No, the status record has already been collected
Only after the parent forks again
Only if the child is restarted
answer: No, the status record has already been collected
questions.explanation: Reaping consumes the pending status record. A later wait cannot collect it again as a still-waitable terminated child.
